title: My agent's plan left me RM8,000 short every month. What now?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #205 | DON'T BLINDLY TRUST AGENTS
excerpt: On a friend's agent's advice, a buyer bought four units with cashback and now owes more than they are worth. Sean explains what went wrong and how to dig out over three to five years.

qa.asker: D, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: D is 32, works in Singapore and saves about RM7,000 a month. In 2019, on the advice of a friend's agent, he bought four investment units: two in Puchong and two in Bukit Mertajam. Each loan is now RM80,000 to RM300,000 more than the unit's market value, and he is about RM8,000 a month short. The agent promised the cashback would cover the instalments, managed the units badly, then handed them back. D's CCRIS record is now damaged, so he can't refinance or get a personal loan.
qa.question: How can he reduce his debt, and should he sell one of the Bukit Mertajam units at a loss?
qa.quote: Not all properties make money, not all agents can be trusted.
qa.answer: Selling now only turns the shortfall into a personal loan. Sean would cut his spending, earn every extra ringgit he can and pay every instalment on time to repair his credit record. He would also fully furnish the units at each change of tenant to lift the rent, and sell only when prices come closer to what he owes.

reasons.title: Overpriced units can't be sold or refinanced
reasons.body: If a unit is worth RM600,000 and he owes RM900,000, selling still leaves RM300,000 owed to the bank. Refinancing only works when the property is worth more than the loan, and a damaged CCRIS or CTOS record shuts that door anyway.

reasons.title: Cashback is the bank's money, not profit
reasons.body: Prices inflated by rebates let him borrow far more than the units are worth. Sean takes extra financing only when the rent he is sure of still covers the larger instalment, and parks spare cash in a flexi account rather than investing it elsewhere.

reasons.title: Furnishing can lift both rent and value
reasons.body: A fully furnished unit rents faster and recovers first. At about RM500 a month per RM100,000 of loan, raising the rent by about RM500 roughly justifies a RM100,000 higher price. He estimates a careful refit of a semi-furnished unit at RM12,000 to RM15,000.

reasons.title: Auction is the last resort
reasons.body: Bidding usually starts about 30% below market value, and whatever is still owed becomes a personal loan. Bankruptcy follows only if that goes unpaid.

actions: Pay every instalment on time for at least six months to clean up CCRIS and CTOS.
Audit his spending, take overtime and side work, and push monthly savings above RM9,000.
Fully furnish each unit in the gap between tenancies, with help from family or friends on the ground.
Check fully furnished rents in each building to see which unit can be sold closest to its loan.
Check his CCRIS and CTOS reports regularly from now on.
qa.caveat: Recovery depends partly on the market, which he can't control, and could take three to five years. Sean sees the lakeside unit in Puchong as the hardest to fix, since even fully furnished it rents for about RM2,500.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #205. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in March 2023. Sean says he works at The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company, and that his advice to fully furnish is not a push for it; owners can do it themselves.
